title: Why 50% off plus 20% more isn't 70% off
description:
Stacked discounts don't add, they multiply. Take 50% off a $200 coat and you're at $100; the extra 20% comes off that new price, so you pay $80, not the $60 that 70% off would give. Each discount leaves a fraction of the price, 0.5 x 0.8 = 0.4, so you pay 40%: 60% off. The order never matters, and the stack always falls short of the sum by the two discounts multiplied (here 10 points).

Numbers checked in code (verify.py), including 100,000 random discount pairs. Black Friday 2026 is 27 November, the Friday after US Thanksgiving (Wikipedia, Black Friday).

beats.say: Half off plus 20%, or 70% off? Pick one.
50 plus 20 is 70, so it feels like a tie. It isn't. One of them is only 60% off.
Your coat is $200 this Black Friday.
Now the extra 20% comes off the new price, not the old one. That's $20. You pay $80.
70% off the full price? You pay $60. $20 less.
So does the order save you? Swap them.
20% off first: $160. Then half: $80. Exactly the same.
Each discount takes a cut of what's left. Half times 0.8 is 0.4. You pay 40%. That's 60% off.
Stacked discounts always land short of the sum. Here, by 10 points.
So, 30% off, then another 30%. What's the real discount?
